episodes.212363: Thunderstorms, a few which were severe, track north-northeast across the plains of northeast Colorado. Hail up to 1.5 inch in diameter, wind gusts to 70 mph and a tornado.
episodes.212398: Clusters of strong to severe thunderstorms dropped southeast into southern middle Tennessee and north Alabama during the afternoon and early evening hours.  Damaging winds were reported in northwest Alabama including the Shoals metro area.
episodes.212404: A slow moving and persistent thunderstorm brought as much as 1 to 3 inches of rain in a short period of time to a small portion of Minnehaha County. This resulted in the flooding and subsequent closure of Hwy 38 between Hartford and Humboldt.
episodes.212413: Scattered thunderstorms that produced heavy rain developed across Middle Tennessee during the afternoon and evening of May 31, 2026. This heavy rain along with slow storm motions across portions of Jackson County caused flash flooding in the Gainesboro area.
episodes.212438: A trough lifted through the western High Plains as a weak convergence boundary drifted eastward into southeast South Dakota during the late afternoon. Near the boundary, a diurnally destabilized air mass focused convective development in a fairly weak shear environment across the lower James River Valley. Thunderstorms largely produced large hail up to ping-pong ball size during periods of stronger updrafts within the storm clusters. Shear concentrated in lower levels and storm interactions combined to produce several brief tornadoes in southeast South Dakota. Slow moving storms also produced spotty heavy rainfall, some of which that fell on areas that received heavy rainfall west of Sioux Falls in the previous night.
episodes.212446: A large waterspout developed in association with convective showers and thunderstorms developing along a reverse cloud line along the Gulf side of the Lower Florida Keys.
episodes.212470: Isolated strong storms produced high winds, hail and flooding in portions of northeast South Dakota. Hail to the size of quarters was recorded 6 miles southeast of the town of Roscoe and near the town of Leola. Additionally, winds were estimated at 60 mph 5 miles north northeast of Leola, with a 59 mph peak wind recorded on the Sand Lake RAWS. The primary impact of these storms was the heavy rainfall around the Leola area. The SDSU mesonet station on the east side of Leola recorded 5.48 inches of moisture with this system. Flooding in the town of Leola impacted many residents with street and basement flooding. 6 to 12 inches of water was observed covering portions of Highway 10 just west of town and heavy equipment was required to move water and debris. Highway 45 south of town was also impassible due to flooding.
episodes.212619: Upslope flow, coupled with disturbances in the flow aloft, yield scattered showers and thunderstorms during the afternoon of the 31st, mainly near the higher terrain. One storm managed to produce damaging winds that uprooted a tree near the Alpine Country Club.
episodes.212681: Very hot temperatures and a dryline allowed scattered thunderstorms to develop on the afternoon of the 31st. Thunderstorms initially developed along this dryline from the northern Rolling Plains into the southern South Plains. The thunderstorms gradually grew upscale into a broken, slow moving line that persisted over the central Rolling Plains into the south-central South Plains through the evening hours. These slow moving thunderstorms primarily produced torrential rainfall but also large hail and damaging wind gusts. Excessive runoff from the prolonged heavy rain flooded fields and inundated area roadways. Some of the heaviest rainfall was along US Highway 87 north of Tahoka in Lynn County. Water over the roadway and a water rescue prompted the closure of the highway. Several additional vehicles became flooded out along US Highway 87. Additional flooding occurred along US Highway 380 west of Post (Garza County) and in northwestern Lubbock (Lubbock County). As storms decreased in intensity late in the evening, a couple of wake lows formed producing severe wind gusts near Slaton (Lubbock County) and Paducah (Cottle County).
episodes.212865: Several slow-moving thunderstorms developed across the southern Nebraska Panhandle and northern Nebraska Panhandle, bringing hail, tornadoes, and torrential rain fall with flooding occuring in Kimball and Dawes Counties. No verification occurred in southeast Wyoming.
episodes.212969: Strong to severe thunderstorms initiated over far southwestern Nebraska and the Nebraska Panhandle during the late afternoon hours of May 30th. As this activity progressed slowly east into the evening hours, numerous large hail and damaging wind gusts were reported. A couple of tornadoes were also reported. Hail up to 3.5 inches in diameter and thunderstorm wind gusts up to 72 MPH were reported.
episodes.213026: A frontal boundary stalled over southeast Georgia on May 29th and gradually dissipated through May 31st as it meandered southward to the Florida-Georgia border. Deep moisture (PWATs 2+ inches) combined with the frontal boundary and passing shortwaves aloft continued a numerous to widespread shower and thunderstorm pattern each day. Light southwesterly flow ahead of the boundary resulted in slow moving downpours in a Gulf sea breeze dominant regime. Heaviest rainfall amounts were near the I-95 corridor where the Gulf sea breeze collided with the pinned Atlantic sea breeze.
episodes.213027: A frontal boundary stalled over southeast Georgia on May 29th and gradually dissipated through May 31st as it meandered southward to the Florida-Georgia border. Deep moisture (PWATs 2+ inches) combined with the frontal boundary and passing shortwaves aloft continued a numerous to widespread shower and thunderstorm pattern each day. Convection was focused along the frontal boundary especially for inland locations from Waycross northward. Light northwesterly steering flow behind the boundary and abundant moisture led to slow-moving downpours.
episodes.213124: Scattered thunderstorms developed in Missouri during the morning of May 31st. As they passed through central Missouri, one cell was able to produce minor flooding in Boone and Moniteau counties. The thunderstorms then congealed before producing a swath of wind damage in southeast Missouri.
episodes.213410: Numerous rounds of strong to severe storms impacted much of the forecast area during the afternoon, evening, and nighttime hours of May 30th. First, a cluster of storms developed across the Flint Hills and progressed eastward across southeast Kansas. These storms produced hail up to half-dollar size and wind gusts estimated to be at least 70 mph. Then, another round of storms developed across portions of south-central and central Kansas producing hail up to ping pong ball size and wind gusts of at least 70 mph. Additionally, a heat burst occurred across portions of central Kansas as storms began dissipating during the nighttime hours, and Salina Regional Airport recorded a non-thunderstorm wind gust of up to 62 mph from the heat burst.
episodes.213435: High water on the Licking River resulted in a fatality.
episodes.213439: A cluster of thunderstorms moved across Lyon County on the evening of May 30, producing sporadic hail around 1 inch.
episodes.213452: Thunderstorms developed along an instability axis across central Kansas during the evening hours of May 29 before pushing east towards the Missouri Ozarks in the morning on May 30. This scattered morning activity remained sub-severe, however additional thunderstorm development occurred in the afternoon and evening hours, leading to several reports of damaging winds uprooting trees, extensive damage to a barn, and hail up to the size of quarters. Additional thunderstorms developed over Kansas during the late evening hours, pushing into central Missouri on May 31 and causing thunderstorm wind damage across Pulaski and Dent counties in the early afternoon.
episodes.213526: A sharpening High Plains dryline in concert with a strong upper level disturbance approaching from the southwest spawned scattered thunderstorms across northeast Colorado during the late afternoon and evening hours on the 30th. Thunderstorms moved north to slightly northwest. Hail up to ping-pong ball size was measured in Yuma County.  A tornado was reported north of Eckley, but caused no damage.  Further south winds from thunderstorms to the west of Yuma County caused a dust storm southwest of Vernon toward the state line.
episodes.213571: Scattered afternoon thunderstorms developed in a moist and unstable air mass with a couple of severe storms.
episodes.213757: During the evening of May 30, bands and clusters of thunderstorms emerged and spread northeastward. Initially, these convective clusters tracked through an axis of higher MLCAPE before migrating toward a region of lower buoyancy across eastern Nebraska and far eastern Kansas. Despite the decrease in buoyancy, the presence of established cold pools associated with the clusters, combined with the strengthening of the nocturnal low-level jet, maintained these thunderstorms into southeast and east-central Nebraska. Shear was rather limited, leading to a popcorn effect where updrafts quickly increased and then decreased in strength. Hail was estimated up to penny sized in Boys Town, NE at 8:14 PM CST and quarter sized near Tamora, NE at 9:16 PM CST. The thunderstorms continued northward and gradually decayed into the evening.
episodes.214336: Thunderstorms produced strong wind gusts along the Brevard County coast.
episodes.214337: A thunderstorm produced a large funnel cloud over Melbourne. There is no evidence that the funnel touched down.
episodes.214672: Heavy rains during the late part of May led to river flooding on the Cache River at the Patterson gage which the minor flood stage at this site would remain in into the month of June.

events.narrative: A waterspout report was relayed via social media of a waterspout along the Gulf side of Cudjoe Key.  The condensation funnel cloud resembled an elephant trunk in size, tilted about 45 degrees off the vertical toward the west, and extended roughly halfway from cloud base to the horizon.  A spray ring was not visible.  The waterspout drifted slowly toward the east.
A few trees were reported to be down on Highway 133 west of Dixon.
A few trees were reported to be down near Highway 28 and Highway PP.
A tree was down on Highway Z near Trophy Lane.
Multiple photos and videos received of a large funnel cloud near downtown Melbourne. There is no evidence that the funnel reached the surface.
Thunderstorm winds estimated to be about 60 mph in magnitude downed large, healthy trees around St. Francois county. One large branch fell onto a metal outdoor pool, bending its frame in Doe Run.

Thunderstorm winds estimated to be about 60 mph in magnitude downed large, healthy branches in and near Fredericktown. Some fell on a residence and damaged its gutters and roof, though the true extent of the damage is unknown. Other large trees and power lines were downed through the county. Notably, winds caused extensive damage across a farmstead near Junction City. A farm outbuilding was collapsed, and a wooden beam was drilled into the top of a garage. Debris was all over the yard, including atop a GMC Denali and Buick crossover. The debris did damage both vehicles.

Several public social media posts and photos indicated numerous roads in and around the community of Emery were underwater as a result of the heavy rainfall. Standing water, at least several inches deep, was also observed in many yards, including some up against structures.

A brief tornado was observed in an open field by a storm chaser around 1 mile north of Bridgewater. The tornado was estimated to touch down around one-half mile north of the Zion Bible Church on the north edge of Bridgewater.  The tornado tracked northeast for less than one minute before it lifted southwest of the intersection of 436rd Avenue and 263rd Street. There were no damage indicators present to derive a rating. The average path width was estimated at 40 yards based on video evidence.

A storm chaser witnessed a tornado develop around 2 miles northeast of Bridgewater. The tornado formed one-half mile south of 263rd Street just west of 437th Avenue. The tornado tracked northeast across open fields for around 3 minutes before it crossed 263rd Street around one-third mile west of 438th Avenue where metal roof panels were ripped off a barn. The tornado continued northeast for a couple more minutes before lifting just west of 438th Avenue. The tornado was rated EF0 with an estimated peak wind of 70 mph and an average estimated path width of 50 yards.
Hail was jagged, with some as long as a quarter, but most of it was pea to nickel sized.

A trained spotter estimated wind speeds close to 60 mph 5 miles north northeast of Leola, however they noted no damage occurred with these high winds.

Heavy rain caused flooding in Gainesboro along Dodson Branch Highway near Dodson Branch School with the nearby creek out of its bank. Damages are not known.
Most hail was pea to quarter sized, but a few were as big as golf balls. Farm fields farther north are more damaged than those at the site.
